title: Why Japan's $20 Billion Airport Is Sinking
sources: Landsat data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey

chapters.title: An Island That Was Not There

paragraphs.text: This is Osaka Bay in 1985. Open water. Ten years later there is an island here, three miles from the shore, with an airport on it. Japan built it from nothing. And it has been sinking ever since.

By the operator's own measurements, the ground under the first island has dropped almost fourteen meters since the fill began. That is forty-five feet, the height of a four-storey building. Last year it went down five centimeters more.

stat.label: Average settlement of the first island since construction began (45 ft)
Settlement of the first island in 2025, average of 17 points

paragraphs.text: Then Japan built a second island beside it. That one is sinking four times as fast.
Thirty-four million passengers used this airport last year. So why did Japan build its airport in the sea, why did the forecasts miss, and how long can it last?

ask.text: Why build an airport in the sea?

paragraphs.text: Osaka already had an airport. Itami sits inland, north of the city, with houses on every side. The first jet landed there in 1964. Almost at once the neighbours began to protest and to sue over the noise, and in the end Japan's supreme court awarded them compensation.
Near Tokyo, the government had tried to build a new airport on farmland at Narita, and met years of protest from the people who lived there. Planners in Osaka did not want a second Narita.

So they looked at the one place where nobody lived: the bay. The first plan put the airport off Kobe. Kobe said no. The site moved south, five kilometers out to sea, placed so that planes would arrive and leave entirely over water, around the clock. The airport's own engineers later called it a radical solution to the noise problems of Itami.

document.text: "Kansai International Airport was built five kilometers out to sea on Osaka Bay as a radical solution to the noise problems of Osaka (Itami) Airport."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: a radical solution to the noise problems

paragraphs.text: We had to decide to build offshore because there were few viable options, an urban planning professor, Hiro Ishikawa, told This Week in Asia last year. There was one problem with the site. There was no land there.

document.text: "We had to decide to build offshore because there were few viable options."
document.source: Hiro Ishikawa, emeritus professor, Meiji University, to This Week in Asia, 2025

paragraphs.text: The water at the site is about twenty meters deep. Under it lies about twenty meters of soft clay, and that clay is seventy percent water. Put weight on it and the water is squeezed out, the way it leaves a sponge. The operator expected this layer to shrink to two thirds of its thickness.

stat.label: Share of water in the soft clay under the bay, by volume
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: Left alone, that would take decades. So the builders gave the water a way out. They drove one million columns of sand into the clay, each twenty meters long, two and a half meters apart. That was more than all of Japan had installed in the thirty-five years before. It worked: a process of decades was over within a year.

stat.label: Sand drains under the first island, 20 m long, 2.5 m apart
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: In 1987 they started a wall around an empty rectangle of sea, built of rubble and forty-eight thousand concrete blocks. This is our own image from May 1989. The wall is finished. Inside it there is still water.

Then came the fill. Soil dredged from the bay, rock quarried from mountains nearby, more barged in from China and Korea, until the new ground was thirty meters deep. A bridge nearly four kilometers long tied the island to the shore. On September fourth, 1994, the airport opened.

stat.label: Depth of the reclaimed ground on the first island
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: But the sand drains reached only the soft top layer. Under it lies something older. For two million years the sea here rose and fell by more than a hundred meters as ice ages came and went, laying down clay, then sand, then clay again. That stack is up to four hundred meters thick. Nobody can drain it. The operator's own page says the airport is managed on the assumption that long-term subsidence will continue.

stat.label: Thickness of the older clay and sand layers under the islands
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

document.text: "...the airport facilities are managed with the assumption that long-term subsidence will continue."
document.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports (3)

paragraphs.text: The planners knew the island would sink, and they piled on enough soil to allow for it. The plan was that after fifty years the ground would still stand thirteen feet above the sea. By 1990, before a single building stood on it, the island had sunk twenty-seven feet instead of the nineteen predicted.

chart.title: Sinking of the first island by 1990

paragraphs.text: A spokeswoman for the operator, Yukako Handa, told Air and Space magazine that the engineers simply could not believe the gap between their laboratory estimates and what the seabed really did. By opening day the ground had already gone down almost ten meters. Parts of the island reached the fifty-year limit within six years, and at least a hundred and fifty million dollars went into raising the seawall.

stat.label: Settlement of the first island before the airport opened in 1994
Spent to raise the seawall as the island sank

paragraphs.text: An island does not sink evenly. So the terminal, a mile long, stands on nine hundred columns, each with its own gauge. When one drops, it is jacked up and steel plates are slid underneath. The middle of the building has a basement, which makes it lighter than the wings, so the builders packed iron ore under it as ballast. It still sank less than its neighbours, and had to be levelled.

stat.label: Columns under Terminal 1, each monitored and jacked up when needed
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: The sinking reached things nobody had drawn. Rain was meant to run off the runway and out to sea through pipes, downhill. As the ground settled, the slope disappeared. The airport installed thirty-seven large pumps to push its own rainwater out, and in 2007 it covered the whole first runway with new asphalt, twenty-five centimeters thick on average, to give the water a slope again.

document.text: "...with the progression of uneven settlement... the angle of the drainage pipes has gradually lessened, hampering the flow of rainwater into the ocean."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: the angle of the drainage pipes has gradually lessened

stat.label: Installed at ten sites, 3,300 cubic meters a minute
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

stat.label: Asphalt laid on Runway A in 2007-2008, 25 cm thick on average

paragraphs.text: And yet the island held. In January 1995, four months after opening, the Kobe earthquake struck about twenty kilometers away and killed more than six thousand people. The airport was not damaged.

One runway was not enough. In 1999 work began on a second island, in deeper water. This time the builders drove one point two million sand drains. This is our image from 2004, with the new island still being filled. Its runway, four kilometers long, opened in August 2007.

stat.label: Sand drains under the second island
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: By the time that runway opened, the seabed under it had already gone down almost twelve meters. It has gone down six more since. In 2025 the second island sank twenty centimeters, four times as fast as the first.

stat.label: Settlement under the second island: 11.71 m before 2007, 5.96 m since

paragraphs.text: An engineering professor at the University of Illinois, Gholamreza Mesri, has studied both islands for years. In a 2015 paper with a colleague he forecast that by the year 2100 the seabed under the first island will have settled about fifteen point seven meters, and under the second, almost twenty-five. The operator makes no such promise. It says only that it will keep measuring, with the guidance of experts.

stat.label: Forecast settlement of the seabed by 2100, first and second island
stat.source: Funk & Mesri, J. Geotech. Geoenviron. Eng., ASCE, 2015

chapters.title: The Sea Comes Over the Wall

paragraphs.text: A sinking island in a typhoon sea needs its walls to keep up. In 2004 a run of typhoons brought the highest tides and waves the airport had recorded. Waves came over the seawall and destroyed a road behind it. The company raised the walls by one to two meters along eleven kilometers.

document.text: "Waves flowed over the airport's seawalls, destroying a road behind the seawall."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: destroying a road behind the seawall

stat.label: Seawalls raised along about 11 km after the 2004 typhoons
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

paragraphs.text: The sea was also coming from below. The island is made of crushed rock, and the water inside it rose and fell with the tide, into basements. So between 2004 and 2006 the company built a wall underground, about thirty meters deep, all the way around the island.

stat.label: Underground cut-off wall around the island, about 30 m deep, 2004-2006
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

paragraphs.text: Then came September fourth, 2018, twenty-four years to the day after the airport opened. Typhoon Jebi pushed the sea over the walls and across a runway. A tanker of about two thousand six hundred tons, the Houn Maru, dragged its anchor and hit the only bridge. By most reports about three thousand passengers were stuck on the island overnight, and left the next morning by boat.

stat.label: Passengers stranded overnight on 4 Sep 2018, by most press reports

paragraphs.text: The walls went up again. Within three years, with planes still landing, the operator raised the seawalls along more than six kilometers, laid wave-breaking blocks along nearly five, and went on raising the first runway.

stat.label: Seawalls raised after Typhoon Jebi; blocks placed along 4.7 km
stat.source: Kansai Airports, via ACI Asia-Pacific, May 2022

paragraphs.text: None of this was cheap. When the airport opened, its cost was put at about eight billion dollars. By 2008, with the repairs, the second island and its runway, the figure was about twenty billion.

The airport carried that as debt, and for years it charged some of the highest landing fees in the world to pay the interest. In 2016 the state handed the running of the airport to a private group led by Orix of Japan and Vinci of France. Two years later that group was paying the transport ministry about three hundred and fifty million dollars a year for the right.

stat.label: Paid each year to Japan's transport ministry for operating rights (2018)

paragraphs.text: And the passengers came. Twenty-six million in 2016. Thirty-four million in 2025, most of them from abroad. A fully loaded Airbus A380, the operator likes to point out, weighs less than three ten-thousandths of one percent of the soil it lands on.

chart.title: Passengers a year
chart.source: Air & Space, 2018; Kansai Airports traffic figures

paragraphs.text: The operator gives no official lifetime for the islands. The first one now sinks a few centimeters a year, not half a meter. We knew from the start that the airport would subside, Professor Ishikawa said, and we considered the various impacts in the design.

document.text: "We knew from the start that the airport would subside, and we considered the various impacts in the design."
document.source: Hiro Ishikawa, emeritus professor, Meiji University, to This Week in Asia, 2025

paragraphs.text: Japan kept building this way. Chubu, near Nagoya, in 2005. Kobe, the city that said no, in 2006. Kitakyushu the same year. All of them on islands made in the sea.
So here is the question. If your city had no room left for an airport, would you build one on the sea, knowing it would sink?

ask.text: Would you build it, knowing it would sink?

youtube.title: Why Japan's $20 Billion Airport Is Sinking
youtube.description: In 1985 this part of Osaka Bay was open water. Japan built an island there, opened Kansai International Airport on it in 1994, and the ground has dropped more than 13 meters since the fill began. From orbit with our own Landsat and Sentinel-2 images we watch the island appear, follow the second island that is sinking faster, and go through the forecasts that missed, the typhoon that cut the airport off in 2018, and what it costs to keep an airport above the sea.
youtube.pinned_comment: If your city had no room left for an airport, would you build one on the sea, knowing it would sink?
